nodes.description: Wild-type yellow fever virus infects vascular endothelial cells and induces a prolonged pro-inflammatory cytokine response that, together with systemic cytokine storm and hepatic synthesis failure of clotting factors, disrupts endothelial barrier integrity, increases vascular permeability, and leads to vasculopathy, capillary leak, thrombocytopenia, hemorrhagic manifestations, acute kidney injury, and shock during the toxic phase.

nodes.description: In the liver, yellow fever virus replicates extensively in hepatocytes and Kupffer cells, inducing direct cytopathic hepatocyte apoptosis (Councilman bodies), lytic necrosis, and microvesicular steatosis, compounded by an unbalanced intrahepatic cytokine storm driven by TNF-alpha, IFN-gamma, and pro-apoptotic TGF-beta from infiltrating CD4+ T cells and activated macrophages.

nodes.description: Single subcutaneous dose of live-attenuated yellow fever 17D vaccine (or a one-fifth fractional dose during emergency mass-vaccination campaigns) induces serum neutralizing antibodies within 2 weeks in most vaccinees and provides decades-long protective immunity via persistent memory B cells and polyfunctional CD8+ T cells. Rare serious adverse events include yellow fever vaccine-associated viscerotropic disease (YEL-AVD; 0.4 per 100,000 doses, CFR 63%) and vaccine-associated neurotropic disease (YEL-AND; 0.8 per 100,000 doses), which are linked to host genetic defects in innate antiviral immunity (such as type I/III IFN pathway defects).

evidence.reference_title: Yellow Fever Virus: Knowledge Gaps Impeding the Fight Against an Old Foe.
evidence.snippet: A strong, antigen-specific T cell response and persistent memory B cell response seem to represent the hallmarks of long-term protective immunity, as YFV-specific memory T cells and IgG antibodies can persist for decades in patient sera

evidence.reference_title: Yellow Fever Virus: Knowledge Gaps Impeding the Fight Against an Old Foe.
